title: Norrie Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Norrie wells have a 60-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock can make drilling costs and results vary widely.
h1: Norrie, Colorado Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
For rural property near Norrie, the local well records show a wide range of conditions. The median reported depth is 60 feet, and the middle half of wells falls between 46 and 98 feet. That does not make every new well shallow: the deepest recorded well reaches 750 feet, and the ground is fractured mountain bedrock.

Most permitted wells are for domestic or household use. Reported production is generally favorable, with a 12.0 gallons-per-minute median among the wells that list a pump yield. Still, only part of the record includes construction, depth, yield, or static-water information, so nearby permits are useful for planning but do not guarantee a result on a particular lot.

sections.heading: Norrie well depth depends on fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
Norrie’s reported well depths are concentrated near the surface: 76% are under 100 feet, while the middle half runs from 46 to 98 feet. The 90th percentile is 290 feet, and the deepest record is 750 feet. That spread is typical of fractured granite and gneiss, where a productive water-bearing fracture may be shallow on one parcel and much deeper on another.

For a driller’s bid, the 60-foot median is a useful starting point, not a promise. A quote should explain the per-foot rate, casing and grout assumptions, pump setting, and what happens if the hole must continue beyond the planned depth. Review wells closest to the proposed building site rather than relying only on the town-wide median.

sections.heading: What Norrie wells produce for household use
sections.html:
Among the 27 permitted wells reporting pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces from 6.2 to 15.0 gallons per minute; 48% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 44% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, while 7% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

Those figures indicate a generally useful local supply for domestic service, but yield is not the same as storage or guaranteed daily delivery. A low-producing well may still work with adequate tank storage, while a strong well does not remove the need for proper pump sizing, pressure equipment, and water-quality testing.

sections.heading: The Norrie water table and what the records show
sections.html:
Only 6 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. Within that group, the median depth to water is 58 feet, and the middle half is tightly grouped from 57 to 60 feet. That gives a useful local snapshot of static conditions, especially when compared with a proposed well depth.

The permit history does not provide enough water-level observations by decade to establish a dropping or rising trend. Do not treat the 58-foot median as a guaranteed pump setting or as proof that the regional water table is stable. Ask for a recent well test and construction report for nearby properties, and have the driller evaluate seasonal conditions at the site.

sections.heading: Norrie drilling history and the contractors in the record
sections.html:
Permit records span several decades, with 18 permits in the 1960s, 14 in the 1970s, 25 in the 1980s, 26 in the 1990s, 20 in the 2000s, 8 in the 2010s, and 10 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. There are 133 permitted wells in the five-mile study area, including 85 recorded as constructed.

The most active names in these records are Shelton Drilling Corporation, Shelton, Wayne, with 49 wells; Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, Shelton, Joe Wayne, with 14; and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc., Shelton, Steve, with 13. Past activity can help identify local experience, but it is not a performance guarantee for a new hole. Confirm licensing, scope, references, and the permit path before work begins.

sections.heading: What a Norrie well may cost to drill
sections.html:
Norrie’s fractured granite and gneiss make depth the main cost variable. The local drilling model uses a rate of $65-$100 per foot. At the 60-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $3,900-$6,000. A finished system, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, models at about $9,900-$18,000.

Those figures are planning ranges, not a fixed bid. A deeper hole, difficult access, additional casing or grout, difficult trenching, or electrical work can change the total. Ask each driller to separate the hole, casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trench, electrical, testing, and permit-related work. A low per-foot number is not comparable if important finish work is excluded.

sections.heading: Norrie risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
The primary well risk is not a uniformly poor record; it is variability in fractured bedrock. The local files include wells from shallow depths to 750 feet, so a dry hole or low-yield outcome remains a site-specific possibility even where nearby wells perform well. Have the seller provide the permit, construction report, pump information, and any yield test.

Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles show 10 historic mine features, with 0 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That is useful screening information, not a substitute for testing. Test raw well water for relevant contaminants, and check septic setbacks, drainfield space, driveway access, grading, and building layout before closing or starting design.

sections.heading: A practical Norrie lot-buying and building plan
sections.html:
Start with the closest permitted wells and separate records by location, depth, yield, and construction status. The study area has 89 wells reporting total depth but only 27 reporting pump yield, so the data is stronger for understanding drilling depth than for predicting production on every parcel. A driller should walk the site and explain the likely target, access route, and contingency if the first interval is unproductive.

For an existing home, inspect the pump, tank, pressure system, water lines, and recent water tests. For vacant land, verify the DWR permit requirements and confirm that the planned home, septic system, driveway, and electrical service can fit together. Domestic wells are the dominant local use, but water rights and augmentation requirements can matter in Colorado, so resolve those issues before relying on a building plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Norrie, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Norrie is 60 feet, and the middle half runs from 46 to 98 feet. However, 15% are between 100 and 300 feet, 6% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 3% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 750 feet, reflecting fractured mountain bedrock variability.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Norrie?
faq.a: The local model uses $65-$100 per foot for fractured granite and gneiss. At the 60-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $3,900-$6,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,900-$18,000. Actual bids depend on depth, access, casing, grout, and site work.

faq.q: How much water do Norrie wells produce?
faq.a: Among 27 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute and the middle half ranges from 6.2 to 15.0 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute. These results are encouraging for household use, but the limited sample means a nearby yield test is more useful than the regional statistic alone.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Norrie, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit record alone, so test the water from the specific well. The mapped area has 0 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, but it also contains 10 historic mine features. Test for contaminants relevant to the property, especially where mining or septic conditions could affect groundwater.

faq.q: Are there active well drillers near Norrie?
faq.a: The most active drillers in the Norrie-area records are Shelton Drilling Corporation, Shelton, Wayne, with 49 wells; Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, Shelton, Joe Wayne, with 14; and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc., Shelton, Steve, with 13. The newest permit year is 2025. Verify current availability, licensing, scope, and references before selecting a contractor.
